title: Near-linear constant-factor minimum-degree spanning trees
formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\), absolute constants \(K,C\ge1\), and an integer \(b\ge0\) such that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\) with \(n\ge2\) and \(m=|E|\), the algorithm outputs a spanning tree \(T\subseteq G\) satisfying \(\Delta(T)\le K\Delta^\star(G)\) in at most \(C(m+n)(\log_2(n+2))^b\) word-RAM operations? Here \(\Delta(T)=\max_{v\in[n]}\deg_T(v)\) and \(\Delta^\star(G)=\min\{\Delta(T):T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\). All constants and the program must be independent of the graph. This is a static construction problem; the graph is supplied once, and no update sequence is part of the input.
why: A low-degree spanning tree supplies a connected backbone while limiting the largest number of connections handled by one vertex. A constant approximation in near-linear time would make a strong structural guarantee available at a cost close to reading the graph. The target is substantially weaker than exact degree minimization, but stronger than bounds whose approximation grows with the graph size. This is a static construction frontier, despite the dynamic setting of the seminar collection.
status_note: Reported resolution: arXiv:2607.11413v1 (13 July 2026), Theorem 1.1, states a deterministic near-linear construction meeting the source’s constant-factor target. The target correspondence, concluding proof and handling of unknown optimum were checked on 14 September 2026, but the full technical proof was not independently verified and no accepted publication of this particular result was confirmed. Status remains uncertain to express that verification limit; it should not be read as a newly certified open problem.

progress.text: The source recalls Fürer and Raghavachari’s additive-one spanning-tree approximation with O(mn)-scale running time.
Saranurak poses the static near-linear constant-factor construction question in Section 4.2, printed page 105, of Seminar 24471.

Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad and Wang’s STOC 2026 paper gives a deterministic additive-one approximation in \(\widetilde O(mn^{3/4})\) time; it is a time improvement rather than a near-linear resolution.

Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad, Saranurak and Wang’s version 1 states Theorem 1.1 with degree \(\lceil(1+\varepsilon)\Delta^\star\rceil+1\) and near-linear time for fixed \(\varepsilon\). Section 8.3.1 concludes the theorem and Appendix A removes assumed prior knowledge of the optimum. This is recorded as a reported resolution pending independent verification of the full proof.

sentences: The input is one connected graph, and the output is a spanning tree with small maximum degree.
The source asks whether a universal constant approximation can be constructed in near-linear time.
This is a static algorithmic question, despite its inherited placement among dynamic graph problems.
A July 2026 preprint states a stronger deterministic guarantee that would settle the target.
The card records that reported resolution and the exact model while keeping independent proof verification separate.

definitions: The vertices are labelled \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), all edges are unweighted unordered pairs of distinct vertices, and the input has no repeated edges. A spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph with vertex set \([n]\) and edge set contained in \(E\); it has exactly \(n-1\) edges. Its degree counts incident tree edges. The minimum defining \(\Delta^\star(G)\) exists because the graph is finite and connected; for \(n\ge2\), it is at least one. Input is an explicit adjacency-list array with vertex offsets, an entry for each endpoint of each edge, and the integers \(n,m\); each identifier or offset occupies one word. Output is an explicit list of the tree’s \(n-1\) endpoint pairs. The algorithm is a single finite program independent of \(n,m\), with words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed integer \(d\ge4\). Each operation reads or writes constantly many addressed words, compares, branches, performs Boolean operations or shifts, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), or divides unsigned words by a nonzero divisor with quotient and remainder. Shifts by at least \(W\) return zero. Work memory initially contains zero. All input access, initialization performed by the program, preprocessing, addressing and output writes are charged; no oracle for the optimum, graph-dependent advice, real arithmetic or random coins is available. The time bound is worst-case for every valid input. Near-linear means the displayed bound with one fixed logarithmic exponent; the approximation factor is one universal constant, not a function of \(n\), \(m\) or the optimum. The deterministic convention makes explicit the type of algorithm in the currently reported resolution.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean establishing the algorithmic existence statement with explicit finite program, approximation constant and time-bound constants, or proving its negation. An affirmative proof must cover every connected input graph and produce the tree itself, without being given \(\Delta^\star(G)\). An estimate of the optimum, a guarantee restricted to dense graphs or large optimal degree, or an additive error growing with \(n\) does not by itself establish a universal constant ratio. This yes/no question does not ask to optimize \(K\) or approximate the integer optimum within \(1/100\). A cited theorem or an unformalized implementation is not a Lean-verified submission.

context_blocks.text: Saranurak’s question in Seminar 24471 concerns one input graph. It asks for a near-linear-time algorithm achieving a constant multiplicative approximation to the minimum possible maximum tree degree. Its occurrence in a seminar about distributed and dynamic algorithms does not add update operations to this particular question.

The classical Fürer–Raghavachari result has additive error at most one, but its \(O(mn)\)-scale running time is much larger than near-linear. Later near-linear constructions allowed additive terms logarithmic in the number of vertices; such terms do not yield a uniform constant ratio when the optimal degree is small.

Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad and Wang’s STOC 2026 result gives an additive-one approximation in \(\widetilde O(mn^{3/4})\) time. It improves the earlier construction time without itself meeting the near-linear target.

The July 2026 preprint by Bhattacharya, Farokhnejad, Saranurak and Wang states a deterministic construction with degree at most \(\lceil(1+\varepsilon)\Delta^\star\rceil+1\) in \(\widetilde O(m/\varepsilon^2)\) time. Its Theorem 1.1 explicitly identifies this as resolving the constant-factor question. For any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\le1\), this degree guarantee implies a universal constant factor because \(\Delta^\star\ge1\).

The preprint’s theorem, concluding proof and treatment of unknown optimum were inspected. Its full collection of technical lemmas and data-structure proofs has not been independently verified in this review, and the checked author record presents it as an arXiv manuscript. The card therefore records a reported resolution with uncertain verification status, rather than asserting that a new open gap remains or certifying a completed proof.
